REMARKABLE PENSION FRAUDS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune
Detroit, Mich., Dec. 10.—Some months ago the Commissioner of Pensions made the discovery that, during the past few years, a large number of applications for pensions for the widows and children of deceased colored soldiers had been filed by parties residing in this city or vicinity. Many of the claims had been allowed, and the claimants had been drawing their pensions regularly. In every instance the claim was made in behalf of the heirs-at-law of some soldier who had been a member of the One Hundred and Second Regiment. Colored Volunteers, enlisted in Detroit. The claims having been proven, they were in due time allowed. Finally something transpired to lead the authorities at Washington to suspect something wrong in connection with these colored pensioners, and Special-Agent F. A. Wardell was accordingly sent here to investigate. He had been here but a few days before he obtained a mass of testimony implicating a colored man named James C. Richardson and Eugene Fecht, a German attorney. The former had acted as the claim-agent and Fecht prepared the papers. Detroit has a certain quarter known as "Kentucky," covering an area of several acres, and in that quarter the residents are almost exclusively colored people. As soon as Wardell and the local officers got their pipes well laid, they had no difficulty in opening communication with "Kentucky," and they soon learned that there were scores of colored women living in that quarter drawing pensions as widows of deceased soldiers, several of whom had been more children when the war closed. As soon as they could be placed, those women were arrested, and there are now twenty dusky damsels in the jail awaiting trial on the charge of defrauding the United States. Numerous "pensioners" filed to the Canadian town of Windsor, across the river. It appears that the originator of this wholesale scheme to defraud the Government was Richardson. He managed to secure a copy of the musterroll of the One Hundred and Second Regiment and took it to Lansing, and had the Adjutant-General give him the names of those killed in action. He would then say to a colored woman that she was entitled to a pension, and readily secure her cooperation. He would then take her to Fecht, who would prepare the papers, and they would be sent to Washington. No claim ever filed by Richardson was disallowed, so thoroughly fortified was he with manufactured evidence. Among those who applied was Richardson's wife, under an assumed name. It is estimated that he has defrauded the Government to the tune of $75,000, which sum, it was charged, was divided between Richardson, Fecht, and the colored applicants, the two men getting the larger share. The trial of the two men has been in progress in the United States Court here all the week, and resulted to night in the acquittal of Fecht and the conviction of Richardson.

BADLY CUT UP.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LOWA CITY, Ia., Dec. 10.—Two men, named Joseph Errott and C. O. Boyd, from River-

Iowa City, Ia., Dec. 10.—Two men, named Joseph Errott and C. O. Boyd, from Riverdale, a town some ten miles south of here, came to this city last evening and stopped at the Buerckle House. They are neighbors, and it seems that an old grudge existed between them. They met in the barn of the Buerckle House, where Errott had a team, when Boyd seized Errott by the whiskers, and an encounter ensued, when the latter at-

backed Boyd with a knife, cutting him perhaps fatally in the abdomen, on the arm, on his head, and ear, inflicting five fearful gashes, from which he bleed badly as he rushed along the street to Dr. Gillett's office, where he was cared for. Errott left for home in the night, but has since been arrested at Riverside, and will be brought back here to-day for examination. They met in the barn alone, and seemingly premeditated to settle their old grudge, where the encounter continued until other parties happened in and separated them.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal., Dec. 10.—When the case of the extradited Mexican Cota came up in the Superior Court this morning, Deputy United States District-Attorney Lovell appeared and stated instructions had been received from Attorney-General Devens for the District-Attorney to represent the United States, maintain the action under the treaty, and endeavor to prevent a collision of the State with the Mexican authorities. THE BELLEVILLE TRAGEDY.
Particulars of the Brutal Murder of McCann, and the Lynching of his Murderer.
In the Esmeralda Herald of the 11th instant a correspondent, writing from Belleville, gives the following particulars of the recent terrible tragedy at that place wherein John McCann was brutally murdered by Charles Marshall, who in turn was summarily hanged by the citizens:

Marshall had been employed in the livery stable here by Gildersleeve, and in Gildersleeve's absence, some time ago, got on a spree and acted very badly, for which cause he was discharged and McCann put in his place. Marshall was still allowed to sleep in the stable, and on the night of the 7th, being on another spree, went to the room of Gildersleeve, took a pistol out of a trunk, and going to the stable, called McCann and commenced to abuse him. McCann simply asked him (Marshall) not to abuse him as he was an old man and wanted no trouble. Then Marshall drew the pistol, and putting it close to the stomach of the old man, fired, the charge burning and tearing the clothes of McCann and making a fearful hole in his body. McCann fell, and then Marshall stamped and kicked him on the head repeatedly, and walking to the back end of the stable returned and kicked him again, doing this for the third time, until he had stamped and kicked the life out of McCann, all the time swearing and abusing him fearfully. Two men happened to be sleeping in the stable that night, and being awakened by the noise, saw the crime committed; but being strangers and unarmed, and Marshall armed and frantic, they were afraid to interfere or make their presence known. After the, crime Marshall replaced the pistol in the trunk and went to his bed in the stable. The other men slipped out and reported the affair, and the next morning Marshall was arrested. All these facts were brought out at the Coroner's inquest.

Citizens generally seemed to think summary punishment ought to be visited upon Marshall, but the town was extremely quiet and no threats were made.

The prisoner was ironed and placed by Clem Ogg in charge of J. S. Longabaugh for the night. Mr. Longabaugh reported that everything was quiet until about 4 A. M., when eight masked and heavily armed men presented themselves at the door of the room where he had the prisoner and, calling Longabaugh out, presented pistols and made him stand aside, one of them telling him they had come for Marshall, not another word being spoken. They then proceeded to gag Marshall, pinion his arms, and throwing a rope over his head, took him to the rear of Farrington's blacksmith shop and hung him to a frame that was there, and then quietly dispersed, no one seeing whence they came or whither they went. There were only eight that entered the room for Marshall but there were quite a number outside who assisted in the hanging when Marshall was brought out. Clem Ogg, the Sheriff, was called out of bed, but seeing the uselessness of resisting a body of armed and determined men, retired again and said nothing.

A woman about 35 years old, wife of a German named Glassma, living on the Meni farm, in Marquette, Green Lake county, Wis., in a fit of temporary insanity killed her babe by cutting its head nearly off. THE HANGING.

The information was at once con-
veyed to the Vigilance Committee,
and at 3 o'clock Thursday morning

HE DIED GAME.

Marshall did not utter a word after his seizure. When asked if he had anything to say, he simply shook his head. He died game—not showing the least sign of weakness.

Both men were single. Marshall was about thirty years of age and McCann nearly double that.

The report that Marshall was taken from Sheriff Ogg and posse is incorrect, according to the Chronicle's information. The fact that Sheriff Ogg is one of the proprietors of the Belleville Hotel, in which Marshall was stopping, may have had something to do with the starting of that rumor.

The cause of the difficulty is unknown.

peter-moore-hempstead-1880-11.A5:
TEXAS FACTS AND FANCIES.
Snow fell for six hours at Dallas on the 5th.
Glanders is prevalent among the horses of Dallas.
LaSalle county was organized at the late election.
The Hebrews of Calvert propose building a synagogue.
Col. J. M. Claiborne, of Galveston is reported fatally sick.
The drive of Texas cattle to Kansas is put down at 359,684.
The new military post to be built at El Paso will cost $350,000.
In McLennan county, Joe Hanks was killed by his half brother Sam McFall.
In Hallettsville a municipal election is ordered for the 18th November, 1880.
The Seventh Day Adventists commence a campmeeting at Dallas November 14.
The Santa Fe railroad is carrying cotton from Cameron to Galveston at $3 75 per bale.
The Santa Fe railroad is carrying cotton from Cameron to Galveston at $3 75 per bale.
The track of the Texas Pacific railroad has been laid twenty miles west of Eastland City.
A brakemar by the name of Schull was killed at Rockdale while attempting to couple cars.
The Age compliments our newly elected sheriff, Ed. Creary. He lived a number of years in Houston.
The Southern Methodist conference at Luling ordained five Mexicans as members of the ministry.
The Longview New Era, Greenback organ, came down to a half sheet in its first issue after the election.
The epizooty has reached San Antonio, and we may look for and be prepared for it in all portions of the state.
There is to be a big railroad meeting at Memphis, November 30, to see about the proposed new road to Texas.

Nine inches of snow fell at Fort Concho on the 5th. Snow fell also at Fort Worth during the whole of the same day.

In excavating under a stone in Columbus, the bones of a human being were found only sixteen inches beneath the surface.

And now the Santa Fe Railroad Company is dickering for a good pile at Waco. Contesting points are notified to raise bids.

Col. A. H. Belo of Galveston has arrived in New York from his European trip, and will reach home the latter part of this month.

Another murder at Heupstead. This time it is Adams, the town marshal, who was shot in the head by a negro named Peter Moore.

Out of eleven hundred and thirty-six votes cast in Granbury, Hood county, Garfield did not receive one, and Texas is more solid than ever.

Penn's ministrations at Dallas have saved 400 souls from perdition. When he gets through with Dallas he may feel encouraged to try Austin.

The body of H. N. Bones was found dead in a mud hole near Fort Worth on the 6th. It is supposed he fell from his wagon and was frozen.

The Age brought out two roosters—its state rooster, fat, smooth, lively and erect; its national rooster, sick and apparently about to kick the bucket.

Many Texas farmers are disgusted with their experience with Northern seed corn. It was three weeks earlier than Texas corn, but small and trifling.
Professor Minor, principal of the normal school for colored pupils at Prairie View, is dead. He was a colored man, and was educated at Oberlin, Ohio.

John McLaughlin, while stealing a ride on the Sunset road, fell to the track, and from injuries sustained by the cars passing over him he died in a few hours.

It is expected that between 1000 and 1500 delegates will attend the great freethinkers' and liberalists' meeting which is to be held at Waco on the 25th of November.

A cattle breeder in Ohio says the only advantage which the Texan steers possess is this, that their flesh when the bones are taken out, can be packed in their horns.

The Belton Journal says it is believed that somebody besides Blandford shared in the money taken from the building association. Such things have been talked of in Austin.

By the ditching of a T. &. P. train near Mineola on the 6th thirteen passengers and two railroad men were slightly injured. W. G. Kirk, an employee of the railroad, is not expected to live.

It is estimated that there are six million acres of sugar land in Texas, which, at a low calculation, would raise if cultivated 6,000,000 hogsheads of sugar and 377,000,000 gallons of molasses.

Amateurs are going to give the people of San Antonio the Opera Martha. Sixty-nine persons will take part in the performance, and the orchestra will be composed of twenty musicians.

The editor of the Mexia Ledger has been notified that Spencer F. Baird, United States fish commissioner, will shortly send to Texas a large number of carp fish for propagation in our ponds and tanks.

It is said another Texas land fraud is being perpetrated in the North, this time called "Pease River City" the plats of which are now being extensively circulated. The site of the city is pretended to be in Hardeman county.

A theatrical manager of New Orleans, hearing of the reputation of little Laura McAllister, of San Antonio, in her role of "Little Buttercup" in the amateur Pinafore company, has made a profer to engage her services.

Moore was placed in jail here for safe keepin, as threats of hauging were liberally indulged in at Hempstead. Moore is a bright mulatto and was in our jail some five years ago having been arrested on a capias. He has served two years in the penitentiary and is a bad negro. He is about 26 or 28 years old.
peter-moore-hempstead-1880-11.A9:
GLOBELETS.
Ex-Congressman Jeremiah Rusk, of Wisconsin, is a candidate for sergeant-at-arms of the next House.

Gen. Thomas Ewing passed through Wooster, O., the other day, en route from New Mexico to New York.

For the first time in more than twenty years we have a President, an ex-President and a President elect, all living.

General Grant is expected to arrive in Washington about the first of next month. He will be given a reception by the citizens of the District.

It is the gosip in Washington that Gen. Harry White, of Pennsylvania, defeated for re-election to Congress, is a candidate for the clerkship of the next house.

Mr. Thomas Hughes is authority for saying that "The Life and Letters of Frederick Denison Maurice," at least the first volume may be expected late in the fall.

Gen. Grant, Senator Conkling and Gen. Arthur have accepted invitations to a "jubilee supper," to be given at Newark, N. J., on the evening of November 22.

A corsage cluster of flowers is now furnished by Parisian dressmakers, with all dresses except the plainest. Sometimes a small bird is perched in these clusters.

A statue of Robert Burns will be erected in Golden Gate park, San Francisco, by the members of the Caledonian club and other Scotch citizens of the Pacific coast.

Mr. Emmons Blaine, a son of Senator Blaine, has left his profession (the law) and gone into the office of the general manager of the Chicago & Northwestern railroad.
Denis Kearney, the agitator, has returned to his dray, in San Francisco. He says that he is out of pocket through politics, and is glad to go to work again in his old line.

Mr. M. H. De Young, who, since the death of his brother, has been the manager of the San Francisco Chronicle, was married recently to Miss Kate J. Deane, of that city.

Costly shoes for wear with fine street costumes are made with tops that roll over and are lined with silk and embroidered to match the costume with which they are worn.

The late William B. Spooner, of Boston, bequeathed $10,000 to the divinity school connected with Harvard university, and $5,000 to the theological school at Meadville, Pa.

A girl only 8 years old was arrested for drunkenness at Lowell. To complete the disgraceful picture, the police let her lie ten hours insensible in a cell without attention.

Dr. John W. Kennion, a practical missionary, not only preaches to the poor of New York, but treats them to free hot coffee and bread from a cart driven through the streets.

Great excitement prevails at Hemstead, Tex., over the killing of Deputy Marshal Adams by Peter Moore. A vigilance committee has been organized, and the lynching of Moore is looked for.

Gen. W. T. Withers has rented Ashland, the old Henry Olay farm, now the property of Kentucky university. He will make it what it was many years ago, a breeding and stud farm.

"Jefferson Davis' Memoirs," it is now stated, will not be given to the public until April. The Appletons have the first volume; in type, but they are delaying the publication until the second volume is ready.

Rev. L. W. Bacon, of Norwich, Conn., has started a new temperance movement in which he recognizes the need of a certain limited sale of spirituous liquors, and also of places of entertainment for young men.

Mr. Thomas Brassey has bought from Sir John Macdonald 64,000 acres of land in Canada, at the foot of the Roeky Mountains. He may now have from 1,200 to 1,600 working tenants, with from "forty to fifty acres each."

Mr. Samuel H. Gladstone, the premier cousin, who came over recently to take a look at us, is now in the Sioux country. He expresses himself as delighted with the West and is inclined to become an American.

Prof. Richard A. Proctor, the distinguished English astronomer, who is now in Australia, states that he will return to England by way of San Francisco and New York, instead of going via the Indian ocean, as was his previous intention.

P. T. Barnum recently received a letter from a man who said he had made a bet that he was not a brother of W. H. Barnum, to which the showman replied he thanked heaven that there was no nearer relationship than that of Adam.

The will of the late Edward M. Barringer, accidentally killed at Zurich, Switzerland, bequeaths most of his real and personal estate to Harvard college, to be invested as a fund for the benefit of the medical school.

The holy synod of Russia has decided upon erecting an orthodox church in the city of San Francisco. The priest of the Russian chapel of New York has recently petitioned the holy synod for permission to erect an orthodox church in that city.

The ex-khedive of Egypt has been abandoned by all the inmates of his harem, with the exception of two coal-black girls of Nubian origin. His funds having been curtailed, he found it impossible to retain his hold upon the fairer complexioned ladies.

The artist Greenough, whose death in Paris was announced last week, was not Mr. Richard S. Greenough, the sculptor, but his son, Gordon Greenough, a young artist of great promise. He was a graduate of Harvard college about ten years ago, and had since lived chiefly abroad.

peter-moore-hempstead-1880-11.A13:
Hempstead.
Special to the Herald.

Hempstead, April 12.—Peter Moore, colored, was placed on trial to-day for the murder of City Marshal J. H. Adams, in November last, and pleaded not guilty.

At 5:30 this afternoon the court adjourned, having secured eight jurors, six colored and two white. Three venires, embracing one hundred and thirty jurors were exhausted of our best citizens. Many of them disqualified themselves because of preconcerted opinions, impressions or prejudices.

Very few colored jurors excuse themselves.

This case is a sad commentary upon our jury system. In the Moore case the state is represented by District Attorney Hanny, County attorney Lipscomb and A. J. Harvey, esq.

The defense by H. M. Browne, esq.

A brisk norther struck here about 5:30 this evening, and fires and shawls are in demand.
peter-moore-hempstead-1880-11.A16:
Hempstead.
Special to the Herald.

Hempstead, April 14.—The jury in the case of Peter Moore, after a retirement of fourteen hours, this morning brought in a verdict of guillity of murder in the second degree, and gave him seven years in the penitentiary. A motion for a new trial in the case of Thomas Ballard, convicted for two years for assault with intent to kill, was overruled. The case of the state vs. George Lawrence, charged with the murder of Thomas Ray, sr., on the night of July 1st, is now on trial.

Heavy frost fell this morning, killing cotton and vegetables.

Cotton seed is very scarce and hard to get, at twenty-five cents per bushel. There is not enough in the county to plant half a crop.

Rain is needed sorely.

store-burning-colfax-1880-12-09.A2:
Murderous Incendiaries.
There are a set of cowardy cut-throats some eight or ten miles southeast of Colfax, on Bayou Philip or Bayou Darro, who richly deserves a term in the penitentiary or justice at the end of a limb. Last Thursday night, about ten o'clock, they set fire to a store owned by two colored men, Israel Smith and Hansom Brisco, and burned it to the ground. The store had goods in it amounting to nearly $800, and the building was worth about $100 more. While the store was in flames several volleys were fired into it. No one was in it at the time, the occupants being at a house several hundred yards away, and too frightened to venture near. This party is evidently the same set who killed a young negro man in the same store early in the fall, by shooting through the walls. Measures should be taken to break up this nest of outlaws, and we hope to see active operations to do so commenced at once. These negroes are entitled to protection, and our community cannot prosper with such a set of cut-throats in it. Israel Smith, one of the store proprietors, says he has no clue as to whether the party consisted of white or black men.

The animus of this act probably was to strike a blow at the "seed cotton" traffic. But it is rather late in the day for that; beside, it is a poor beginning to make on a couple of timid negroes, who are only following the lead of a dozen white men who have done the same business all the past fall.
store-burning-colfax-1880-12-09.A3:
Another Version.
Under the heading of "Murderous Incendiaries," last week, we published an account of the burning of a "seed cotton" store in this parish, and made some severe strictures about the firing of guns, etc., on that occasion. In justice to our people, and without any desire to harm the colored men who owned the building, we now state that it is the common report that the owners themselves had a hand in burning it, for the purpose of getting the insurance on the concern, and that they tried to give the affair the color of an "outrage" by firing off guns. The store was in a lonely spot in the woods, very favorable for the carrying out of such a scheme. The probabilities are as much in favor of this version as the first one published.

SUMMARY OF STATE NEWS.
Gleanings from the Louisiana Press.

Thibodaux Sentinel: Four plantations that have completed rolling have made 555 hogsheads of sugar against 370 hogsheads in 1879.

Caldwell Herald: A cutting affray took place at Brown's store in which a man named Ainsworth was probably fatally wounded by Jim Smith.

Clinton Patriot Democrat: A Mr. Hoffmeister, a tailor of this place, who was living alone in a building on the Dominique Zimmerman premises, fell in the fire Saturday night and was burned to death.

St. Bernard Eagle: Stephen S. Cole, a colored boy, is under arrest for shooting and instantly killing Ben Valere, another colored youth, on the Olivier plantation. Valere was shot because he refused to go hunting with Cole and several other boys.

Claiborne Guardian: The dwelling-house of P. C. Collier was destroyed by fire Sunday night with all its contents. The family did not even save their wearing apparel. The house was large and well furnished. The loss is a heavy one.

Concordia Eagle: In the case of the State vs. Ashburry Harris a colored man, for the alleged murder of R. P. Derbin, white, a lessee on one of Mr. Yznaga's plantations, coming up on preliminary examination, Judge Hough held that the killing was justifiable and discharged the prisoner.

Baton Rouge Advocate: Mr. R. H. Burke, the contracting carpenter, has pushed ahead his work on the State-House with surprising energy. He has the House of Representatives and a number of the other rooms near enough completed for the plasterers to begin lathing. In a few days he will also have the Senate chamber near enough done for the lathing.

Livingstonian: A party of surveyors arrived last week at Maurepas for the purpose of continuing the survey of the Conway tract of the Houmas claim, above Tiger Bluff, and extending as high up the Amite river as Cornett's Mill—in ownership 8 and 9, range 5. It is to be hoped that ere many months shall have passed away, the settlers on the disputed territory may be satisfied as to their claims.

Morehouse Cotton Plant: Messrs J. Sharp, W. L. Doss, and James B. Williams, of this parish, started on Monday last for Alabama for the purpose of proenring colored laborers to work on their plantations next year. They will probably be able to bring on about one hundred and fifty, and this parish will then lack just 9850 more. Ten thousand laborers, in addition to what we already have, would not be one too many for this parish. We need labor, and we need it badly.

The Negro was pursued and shot to death, and proved to be a murderer who escaped from jail in Terrebonne sometime ago. The verdict of the Corner's jury was that he was killed by pasties unknown. A two year old Negro child was accidentally drowned in a hole of water near the store of J. Freyhan & Co., Thursday evening.
